citeinfo.title: LiDAR and paleoseismology solve 140-yr old earthquake mystery in the Pacific Northwest USA - source tabular data and images for 1872 Chelan earthquake fault scarp study

descript.abstract: This dataset contains LiDAR DEMs, magnetic field images and data, radiocarbon results, tree ring counts, and fault scarp trench logs.
descript.purpose: These data were collected to identify and describe the source rupture for the December 14 1872 earthquake near Chelan, Washington.

procstep.procdesc:
For aeromagnetic data: The interpretation of magnetic anomalies was based on a low-altitude, high-resolution airborne survey of the magnetic field flown in 2011 by a geophysical consulting firm under contract to the U.S. Geological Survey. Measurements of the total magnetic field were made along parallel lines oriented east-west and spaced 400 m apart. Survey altitude was nominally 250 m above ground but varied significantly over rugged terrain. Survey altitude was <200 m over the relatively flat plateau southeast of the scarp, 700 to 1000 m over the Columbia River, and 740 to 860 m directly over the scarp. Total field measurements were reduced to total-field anomaly values by subtraction of the International Geomagnetic Reference Field (IGRF). Various well-established methods (Blakely, R.J., 1996, Potential theory in gravity and magnetic applications: Cambridge University Press, 464 p.) were used to facilitate our interpretation, including reduction to the pole to remove magnetic anomaly asymmetries caused by non-vertical magnetization and non-vertical ambient field, filtering to emphasize anomalies caused by shallow magnetic sources, and boundary analysis to automatically map contacts between near-surface rocks with contrasting magnetic properties. These derivative products were used together and with topographic and geologic databases to interpret lithologic contacts lying near and parallel to the scarp and to extrapolate those contacts beyond the limits of the scarp.
For paleoseismic trenches: Trenches across the scarp were excavated by hand using picks and shovels to depths of ~1.3m. We logged stratigraphic contacts and structural features on rectified photomosaics of each trench. After cleaning the trench walls using hand tools, we gridded the walls using laser levels and established horizontal and vertical fiduciary marks using nails and string. Photomosaics were created by taking digital photographs of each grid cell and digitally stitching rectified photographs in Adobe PhotoShop CS6. Photomosaics were printed on 24" wide paper, mounted on foam boards and covered with acetate. Stratigraphic contacts, faults, and other field observations were recorded on the acetate in permanent marker. The acetate was scanned and a digital file imported into Adobe Illustrator for final trench log preparation.
